title: Dried grapes
subtitle: Raisins and passito
objectives: Explain how dried grapes can make dry wines

steps.title: Drying after picking
steps.body: Grapes can be dried after harvest, on straw mats, in lofts or racks, or in the sun. Over weeks or months they lose 30 to 50% of their weight. The method is ancient and found all around the Mediterranean. In Italy it is called appassimento, and the wines are called passito.

steps.title: Sweet and dry
steps.body: Most dried grape wines are sweet: Vin Santo from Tuscany, Recioto della Valpolicella, Sicily's Passito di Pantelleria, and Spain's Pedro Ximénez, dried in the sun. But fermentation can run to dryness too. Amarone della Valpolicella is made from dried Corvina grapes fermented nearly dry, giving a powerful red of around 15 to 16% alcohol.

steps.prompt: Amarone is made from dried grapes, but fermented to be nearly ____.
steps.explanation: Unlike Recioto, Amarone's fermentation continues until almost all the sugar is gone, giving a powerful, dry red.

steps.title: Why drying changes flavour
steps.body: Drying doesn't just concentrate sugar. The berries start to oxidise and dry out, adding raisin, fig, dried cherry and chocolate notes. Some grapes get a touch of botrytis in drying lofts too. The result is rich, often high in alcohol, and long-lived.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to its region.
steps.explanation: Drying grapes is a Mediterranean tradition, from Spain to Sicily.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Drying grapes after picking concentrates sugar, acid and flavour
Vin Santo, Recioto and Pedro Ximénez are sweet dried grape wines
Amarone is made from dried grapes but fermented nearly dry
